name: Globus (University of Chicago)
subcategory: research data transfer, sharing and automation service (nonprofit SaaS)
origin_detail: Grew from the open-source Globus Toolkit (GridFTP and related grid software) developed by Ian Foster's team; the Globus team's 2005 GridFTP paper won the SC25 Test of Time Award. The current hosted service (site copyright from 2010) is 'developed and operated as a not-for-profit service by the University of Chicago' and works closely with Argonne National Laboratory facilities. The old toolkit lives on as the community Grid Community Toolkit, 'based on a fork of the Globus Toolkit'.
openness_notes: The original Globus Toolkit was open source (its community fork, GCT, is Apache-2.0). The current product is a hosted service: free basic transfers for users at non-profit research institutions, paid organisational subscriptions for advanced features; client SDKs are Apache-2.0. Scored 1 (only peripheral SDKs/clients open).

license_history.license: Globus Toolkit: open source (community fork GCT is Apache-2.0)
license_history.note: Toolkit end-of-support date not confirmed on fetched pages

relicensing_events.outcome_note: Grid users kept GridFTP/GSI/MyProxy via the community fork while Globus moved to a sustainable SaaS model.

risk_events: Abandoning the self-hosted open toolkit for a hosted service pushed parts of the grid community to maintain their own fork (GCT).
27 May 2026: Globus began offering free Standard subscriptions to non-profits with annual research budgets under $4 million, shifting more of the cost onto larger subscribers.
robustness: Run by a university as non-profit infrastructure with a subscription base, Internet2 NET+ membership (Jan 2025) and deep integration with DOE facilities (Argonne's APS and ALCF, NERSC's Perlmutter, OLCF's Frontier). Single operator, closed service: users depend on UChicago's continued operation.
physical_science_relevance: The standard tool for moving large instrument and simulation data between US national labs, light sources and universities; used for near-real-time X-ray (XPCS) data flows from Argonne's upgraded APS to supercomputers (Jan 2026) and alongside Argonne's AI inference service for science (May 2026).
openness_effect_assessment: Globus moved from open software to a freemium hosted service to become financially sustainable, a rare example of academic infrastructure deliberately 'closing' the product while keeping access free for most researchers. The move worked at scale (1 exabyte and 150,000+ users by 2020) but left the open code to a community fork.
key_takeaway: Globus is the freemium counter-model in open science infrastructure: a university-operated service that charges institutions for advanced features while keeping basic transfers free for non-profit researchers. It shows that 'open science' infrastructure can be sustained by subscriptions rather than grants, at the cost of open-source control.
funding_sources: Institutional subscriptions (Starter, Standard, High Assurance, BAA, connectors)
